title: Five marks of good speech
hook: spoken at the right time, true, gentle, beneficial, with a kind heart (AN 5.198)
tomorrow: The stick in the baby's throat

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma vaca, right speech, with four guards at the door of the mouth. Your line: four guards.

You've been rehearsing it in the shower for three days: the sentence you need to say to your roommate about the dishes, or to your father about his driving, or to a friend about the thing she keeps doing. Every version is either so soft it means nothing, or so sharp it'll start a fight. Long ago, the Buddha gave a checklist for exactly this moment. It has five boxes, and it would fit on a sticky note on the bathroom mirror.
screen: `THE SENTENCE IN THE SHOWER.` → `TOO SOFT, OR TOO SHARP.` → `A STICKY NOTE WITH FIVE BOXES.`

segments.voice: In a short sutta in the Numbered Discourses, the Buddha says that speech with five qualities is well spoken, blameless, and not faulted by the wise. Spoken at the right time. Spoken truly. Spoken gently. Spoken for benefit. And spoken with a mind of goodwill. Hold your shower sentence up to them and something shifts. Truth isn't first on this list. Time is. A true thing said at the wrong moment, in the middle of the argument, in front of the whole table, at eleven at night, can land like a stone. Gently translates the Pali saṇha: smooth, soft, fine. It's about how the words feel to receive, not only what they say. For benefit means the words are going somewhere good, for the listener, and not only for your own relief. And the last mark isn't about the words at all, but the heart they come from. You could say perfectly chosen words with quiet contempt underneath, and this list would catch it. The same five turn up in the simile of the saw, turned around. There the Buddha lists them as ways other people may speak to you: at the right time or not, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, helpfully or not, with goodwill or with hate. And the training is to stay steady either way. So the list cuts in both directions. It's what to aim for when you speak, and not a test everyone else must pass before you'll stay kind.
screen: `FIVE MARKS OF WELL-SPOKEN SPEECH.` · `TIME COMES FIRST.` · `GENTLE, HELPFUL, FROM GOODWILL.` · `THE LIST CUTS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `TRUE, TIMELY, KIND.`

segments.voice: Bring back a sentence you've been rehearsing, or one you'll need to say soon, and hold it to the five, a breath or two for each: is it the right time, is it true, is it gentle, will it help, is it coming from goodwill? If one box stays empty, don't force it; just notice which one. Then rest, and let the sentence wait in the quiet until it's ready.
Subhasita vaca, well-spoken speech. Timely, true, gentle, beneficial, and from a mind of goodwill. From the Numbered Discourses, in the book of fives.
Your line: true, timely, kind. On this list, time comes even before truth. That's day three hundred sixty-six.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often offer these five as questions to ask before speaking, and monastics hear the same five in the simile of the saw as a training in staying steady when others speak badly to them.

fork.setup: your friend's wedding toast ran far too long. she asks how it went while the cake is being cut. what do the five marks suggest?
options: find a quiet moment later, if it would help her.
fork.reveal: AN 5.198 puts the right time first: a true word still waits for its moment, and it has to be helpful and kindly meant.

original.note: Pali subhāsitā vācā: well-spoken speech, the kind with all five marks.

chat.says: If something's true, shouldn't I just say it right away?
options: Not always; in the Buddha's five marks, the right time comes even before truth.
Yes; once it's true, how and when you say it doesn't really matter.
Only if they'll be glad to hear it; otherwise a true thing stays unsaid.
chat.meaning: AN 5.198 lists five marks of well-spoken speech, and time comes first: a true thing said at the wrong moment can land like a stone.
